title: Gender Identity
scope: Whether gender identity or birth sex should govern law and shared life: legal recognition, sports, single-sex spaces, and medical care for minors.

overview.summary: When a person’s gender identity and birth sex differ, which should govern documents, sports, single-sex spaces and care for minors?
overview.scope_covered: Legal sex on documents and in equality law, eligibility for female sports, bathrooms, changing rooms, shelters and prisons, and youth medical care as one arena where the question is decided.
overview.scope_excluded: The full clinical evidence on youth transition, identity politics in general, pronouns and speech law, whether mental-health diagnoses are expanding too far, and differences of sex development, which raise a separate eligibility question.
overview.why_now: On June 30, 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that states may limit girls’ and women’s school sports teams to biological females, reading “sex” in Title IX as biological sex. The ruling cited the IOC’s March 2026 policy limiting its female category to biological females.
overview.why_now_source_label: Supreme Court of the United States

stats.label: What Americans say determines whether someone is a man or a woman
stats.note: In November 2025, 67 percent of US adults said sex at birth determines whether someone is a man or a woman and 31 percent said it can differ from sex at birth.
stats.detail: The figures come from a survey of 10,357 adults taken November 17 to 30, 2025. Pew has asked the question in the same form since 2017, and the share has risen in every wave: its June 2022 report put it at 54 percent in 2017, 56 percent in 2021 and 60 percent in 2022. The answer sorts views on much else: in the same survey, 89 percent of those who said sex at birth determines gender were uncomfortable with transgender athletes on teams that do not match their birth sex, against 37 percent of those who said gender can differ. The question measures a belief about what makes someone a man or a woman, not a policy preference, and it does not ask how people should be treated; the same public backs protections against discrimination for transgender people.

stats.label: Americans aged 13 and older who identify as transgender
stats.note: About 2.8 million Americans aged 13 and older, 1 percent, identify as transgender, from 3.3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds to 0.3 percent of those 65 and older.
stats.detail: The Williams Institute at UCLA School of Law combined two federal health surveys that ask people directly whether they consider themselves transgender: the CDC’s Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System for 2021 to 2023 and its Youth Risk Behavior Survey for 2021 and 2023. Between the youngest and oldest groups, the share is 2.7 percent at ages 18 to 24, 1.4 percent at 25 to 34 and 0.4 percent at 35 to 64. Among the 2.1 million transgender adults, roughly a third each are transgender women (32.7 percent), transgender men (34.2 percent) and nonbinary (33.1 percent). The steep age gradient is the most debated feature of these data. The institute’s earlier analysis of the 2017 and 2019 youth surveys put the youth share at 1.4 percent, but it warns that its sources and methods changed and the two estimates should not be read as a trend. Gallup’s 2025 telephone polling found 9 percent of US adults identify as LGBTQ+, about 12 percent of them as transgender.
stats.source_label: Williams Institute, UCLA School of Law (August 2025)

stats.label: US states that bar transgender students from school sports matching their gender identity
stats.note: As of October 2026, 27 states bar transgender students from teams matching their gender identity and 26 ban medical transition for minors; 22 plus DC outlaw gender-identity job discrimination.
stats.detail: The counts come from the Movement Advancement Project, a think tank that supports transgender rights and keeps the most widely used state-by-state tracker; each type of law has its own page there. On the same tracker, 21 states restrict transgender people’s use of bathrooms and facilities, and 21 plus the District of Columbia explicitly ban discrimination based on gender identity in public accommodations. The sports figure matches the Supreme Court’s own count of 27 states in its June 2026 opinion; two more states restrict sports participation by regulation or agency policy. One more state bans surgery only for minors, which is why KFF’s tracker, updated September 29, 2026, counts 27 states limiting youth gender-affirming care. In six states and one territory, providing banned care is a felony. About half of transgender youth aged 13 to 17 live in states with sports bans. The map is close to a partisan one: nearly every restricting state is Republican-led, and nearly every state with explicit protections is Democratic-led.
stats.source_label: Movement Advancement Project, Equality Maps (updated October 3, 2026)

stats.label: US high school students who attempted suicide in the past year, by gender identity
stats.note: In 2023, 25.9 percent of transgender high school students reported attempting suicide in the past year, against 11.0 percent of cisgender girls and 5.3 percent of cisgender boys.
stats.detail: The 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey was the first in which the CDC asked a nationally representative sample of high school students whether they were transgender. Transgender students also reported far higher rates of seriously considering suicide (52.9 percent, against 24.0 for cisgender girls and 12.1 for cisgender boys) and of persistent sadness or hopelessness (71.9 percent, against 50.5 and 26.0). Every camp cites these figures, for different conclusions. Those who favor recognition and affirmation read them as the product of stigma, rejection and bullying that inclusive policy reduces. Those who favor caution read them partly as a sign that gender distress often comes with other mental-health conditions that need treatment in their own right; a Finnish national register study (Ruuska and colleagues, BMJ Mental Health, 2024) found that the higher suicide mortality of young people referred to gender services was no longer statistically significant once their psychiatric treatment history was taken into account, a reading transgender advocates dispute. The survey is cross-sectional and cannot show what causes the gap.
stats.source_label: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, MMWR Supplements (2024)

stats.label: European countries that allow legal gender change by self-declaration
stats.note: In 2026, 12 of the 49 countries tracked by ILGA-Europe let people change their legal gender by self-declaration, without a medical diagnosis or other gatekeeping.
stats.detail: The twelve are Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Luxembourg, Malta, Norway, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland. ILGA-Europe, a federation of LGBTI organizations, lists 12 other countries with no functioning legal or administrative process: Albania, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Georgia, Hungary, North Macedonia, Monaco, Russia, San Marino, Slovakia and the United Kingdom. The British entry reflects ILGA-Europe’s own criteria. As of 2026, the UK grants gender recognition certificates under its 2004 Act, which require a medical diagnosis and two years living in the acquired gender, and the Ministry of Justice reported 1,900 applications in 2025–26; a certificate no longer changes a person’s sex for the purposes of the Equality Act.

stats.label: Elite male performance advantage over females, by event
stats.note: Elite men outperform elite women by about 11 to 13 percent in running, swimming and rowing, 18 percent in jumping events and 33 percent in vertical jump.
stats.detail: These gaps are why sport has a protected female category at all, and every side accepts that they exist between males and females who have gone through their own puberty. They open at puberty under the influence of testosterone; the review puts the male advantage at 31 to 37 percent in Olympic weightlifting, depending on weight category, and 162 percent in punch power. The dispute is whether they persist after a transgender woman lowers her testosterone. Hilton, a developmental biologist, and Lundberg, a physiologist, reviewed the studies available in 2020 and concluded that 12 months of suppression below 10 nanomoles per liter, then the standard eligibility rule, reduced muscle mass by only about 5 percent, leaving most of the male advantage intact. Some sports bodies distinguish athletes who went through male puberty from those who did not, as World Aquatics did in 2022; the IOC’s 2026 policy instead excludes all athletes whose genes show male sex development. The figures are for elite athletes; gaps at youth and recreational levels vary and are less studied.

stats.label: Transgender women’s fitness-test edge over other women in the US Air Force
stats.note: After two years of feminizing hormones, transgender women in the Air Force still ran 1.5 miles 12 percent faster than other servicewomen, down from 21 percent; their push-up and sit-up edge vanished.
stats.detail: This is one of the few studies to follow the same people over time, using routine military fitness tests and medical records of 46 transgender women and 29 transgender men. It is the main evidence that some advantages, especially in endurance running, last well beyond the one year of testosterone suppression that sports bodies once required, while strength-endurance measures such as push-ups and sit-ups converge within two years. The participants were service members, not competitive athletes, and the tests measure fitness rather than performance in a sport.
stats.source_label: Roberts, Smalley & Ahrendt, British Journal of Sports Medicine (2021)

stats.label: US support for policies on transgender people
stats.note: In February 2025, 66 percent of Americans favored birth-sex sports teams, 56 percent a ban on transition care for minors, and 56 percent protecting transgender people from discrimination.
stats.detail: Each row is a separate question, so the shares do not add up, and one person can favor both a sports restriction and protections against discrimination in jobs, housing and public spaces; that is the most common combination. Every restriction gained 6 to 10 points since Pew’s 2022 survey: birth-sex sports teams from 58 percent, a ban on gender-transition care for minors from 46, birth-sex bathrooms from 41 and a ban on teaching about gender identity in elementary schools from 41. Support for protecting transgender people from discrimination fell 8 points, from 64 percent. Requiring health insurers to cover transition care, never popular, fell from 27 to 22 percent, with 53 percent opposed. The public is closely divided on bathrooms (49 percent favor, 26 oppose) and on elementary-school teaching (47 favor a ban, 34 oppose). The survey covered 5,097 adults from February 10 to 17, 2025.

stats.label: Transgender athletes in US college sports known to the NCAA president
stats.note: In December 2024, NCAA president Charlie Baker told a Senate committee he knew of fewer than 10 transgender athletes among the 510,000 athletes in NCAA sports.
stats.detail: Baker, a former Republican governor of Massachusetts, gave the figure in answer to a question from Senator Dick Durbin; it is a count of athletes known to the association’s leadership, not a census. Those who favor inclusion cite it to argue that the issue is tiny in numbers and that statewide bans target a handful of children. Those who favor a sex-based category reply that fairness is decided race by race and roster spot by roster spot, that a few prominent cases, such as swimmer Lia Thomas’s 2022 NCAA title, affected many female competitors, and that the principle matters regardless of numbers. In February 2025, after an executive order on women’s sports, the NCAA limited competition in women’s sports to athletes assigned female at birth.

stats.label: Americans who want birth sex, not gender identity, on government IDs
stats.note: In May 2025, 66 percent of Americans said birth sex rather than gender identity should be listed on government documents such as passports and driver’s licenses.
stats.detail: Gallup’s telephone survey of 1,003 adults, taken May 1 to 18, 2025, with different wording from Pew’s, found 69 percent saying transgender athletes should only play on teams matching their birth sex. Support for letting athletes play on teams matching their gender identity fell from 34 percent when Gallup first asked in 2021 to 26 percent in 2023 and 24 percent in 2025, with the drop concentrated among Democrats and independents. About 90 percent of Republicans favored birth sex for both sports and documents; Democrats were split, with 54 percent preferring that documents show current gender identity. A separate question asks whether changing one’s gender is morally acceptable, not how law should treat it: 40 percent said acceptable and 54 percent morally wrong. Views on transgender people serving openly in the military did not align with the Trump administration’s ban, so the preference for birth sex in some domains is not a blanket position.

stats.label: Support for transgender-inclusive policies, average across countries
stats.note: Averages of 73 percent across 26 countries backed protecting transgender people from discrimination and 50 percent teen care with parental consent; 22 percent across 23 backed sports by identity.
stats.detail: On sports, 48 percent across the 23 countries were opposed, and no country had a majority in favor. Support for gender-identity-based eligibility fell from 32 percent in 2021 to 27 percent in 2024 and 22 percent in 2025 and 2026, including in once-supportive Spain, from 50 to 31 percent; US support was 21 percent and Britain’s 15. Agreement that teenagers should be allowed gender-affirming care fell from 59 percent in 2023. On protection from discrimination, the United States (71 percent) and Britain (74) sit near the average, with Thailand highest (87) and Poland lowest (58). On adolescent care the English-speaking countries are among the least supportive: 40 percent in the United States, 37 in Britain and 43 in Canada, against 79 in Thailand and 64 in Italy. The online survey covered 19,019 adults under 75, April 24 to May 8, 2026; in several middle-income countries its samples are more urban and educated than the general population.
stats.source_label: Ipsos, LGBT+ Pride 2026 (26-country Global Advisor survey)

stats.label: Studies on puberty blockers rated high quality in the York systematic review
stats.note: A University of York review rated 1 of 50 studies on puberty blockers for gender-dysphoric adolescents high quality, 25 moderate and 24 low; critics say it judged the evidence too strictly.
stats.detail: The review was one of eight commissioned by England’s Cass Review of children’s gender services, which published its final report in April 2024; NHS England had stopped routine prescription of puberty blockers for gender dysphoria outside research the month before. The York team found consistent evidence that blockers suppress puberty and that bone density fell during treatment, but limited or inconsistent evidence on gender dysphoria, mental health, body satisfaction, cognitive development and fertility. Similar reviews in Finland and Sweden had earlier led those countries to restrict the treatment, and a US Department of Health and Human Services report in 2025 reached similar conclusions. American medical associations including the American Academy of Pediatrics reject the view that the care is unsupported, and a 2024 response from the Integrity Project at Yale Law School argued that the Cass Review held the evidence to a stricter standard than is usual in pediatric medicine. In February 2026 the American Society of Plastic Surgeons recommended delaying gender-related surgery until at least age 19 (STAT, 2026).
stats.source_label: Taylor and colleagues, University of York, Archives of Disease in Childhood (2024)

stats.label: Transgender prisoners in England and Wales, by prison estate
stats.note: On March 31, 2025, England and Wales held 339 transgender prisoners: 275 in men’s prisons, 245 of them transgender women, and 64 in women’s prisons, 61 of them transgender men.
stats.detail: Prisons are the single-sex space where the stakes are starkest, because residents cannot leave and some have committed violent or sexual offenses. Most transgender women in England and Wales are held in the men’s estate; the other three people in women’s prisons were a mix of transgender women, nonbinary people and other identities. The count rose 15 percent in a year, from 295, against almost no change in the overall prison population, and the prison service says it likely undercounts, because not every transgender prisoner declares it. Nine further prisoners held gender recognition certificates and are excluded. In the United States, a January 2025 executive order directed that “males are not detained in women’s prisons,” and in September 2026 the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to let the Bureau of Prisons stop providing hormone treatment to inmates with gender dysphoria (SCOTUSblog, 2026).
stats.source_label: HM Prison and Probation Service, Offender Equalities Annual Report 2024/25

stats.label: People in England and Wales whose gender identity differs from their sex registered at birth
stats.note: In the 2021 census, 262,000 people in England and Wales, 0.5 percent of those 16 and over, said their gender identity differed from their sex at birth; the figure has since lost accredited status.
stats.detail: The 2021 census was the first in England and Wales to ask about gender identity, and what followed became part of the debate over how sex and gender should be recorded. Patterns in the data, such as unexpectedly high rates among respondents with limited English, suggested many people had misread the question, and in September 2024 the Office for Statistics Regulation agreed to reclassify the estimates as “official statistics in development.” Scotland’s census, which asked a differently worded question, did not show the same pattern. Women’s-rights groups had argued from the start that surveys should record sex and gender identity separately rather than letting one stand in for the other, and the 2025 Sullivan review for the UK government recommended that public bodies collect data on biological sex by default.

questions.text: When the law sorts people as men or women, should it go by birth sex or by gender identity?
questions.why: Both sides agree that sex and gender identity are different and usually coincide. They split over which one words like “woman” and “sex” should track in law when the two come apart.
questions.detail:
No study can settle this, because it is a choice about what legal categories are for: recording a bodily fact that matters for some purposes, or recognizing how people live and are seen. Those who favor birth sex point to the many laws that exist because of sex, from separate sports, shelters and prisons to sex-discrimination law, pregnancy protections and data on women’s pay, health and safety. If “woman” means anyone who identifies as one, they argue, those protections lose their object, and an inner identity cannot be verified or applied consistently.

Those who favor gender identity point to the daily cost of a mismatched classification for someone who lives and is seen as a woman or a man: exposure, harassment and exclusion every time a document is checked. Most social life never involves chromosomes or birth certificates, they argue, so treating people as they live is how society already works, and where a bodily difference genuinely matters, as in some medical settings, it can be handled on its own terms. Many people answer differently by setting, which is why each arena is argued on its own.

questions.text: Does a transgender woman who has lowered her testosterone keep a meaningful athletic advantage?
questions.why: Everyone accepts that male puberty builds a large performance advantage. The dispute is how much survives testosterone suppression, and the studies are few, small and often of non-athletes.
questions.detail:
Those who say the advantage persists note that lowering testosterone does not undo height, limb length, skeletal structure, heart and lung size or hand and foot size built during male puberty, and that elite results are separated by fractions of a percent, so even a small residual edge can decide a race. A sex-based category, on this view, does not need to show that every transgender woman would win; it exists because the sexes differ on average, the same logic that excludes men who are slower than many women.

Those who say the advantage is largely removed answer that testosterone is the main driver of male performance and that lowering it reduces muscle, hemoglobin and strength; a larger frame is not always an advantage once strength falls relative to body mass. Transgender girls who took puberty blockers never go through male puberty at all, and blanket rules treat a varied group as one. The answer also varies by sport, by measure and by whether an athlete went through male puberty. The IOC’s 2026 rule turns on sex development rather than identity, so it also reaches some athletes with differences of sex development. The US Supreme Court called the question “the subject of ongoing medical and scientific debate” and held that it would not change the constitutional answer either way. Even a settled answer would leave a value question: how much residual advantage is too much.

questions.text: Should women’s spaces be separated by sex or by gender identity when privacy and inclusion conflict?
questions.why: Bathrooms, changing rooms, shelters, hospital wards and prisons are separated for privacy, dignity and safety, and both sides invoke those same reasons. The fight is over who bears the cost of uncertainty.
questions.detail:
Most of the conflict is not about whether transgender women as a group are dangerous. One side holds that women undressing, sleeping, giving birth or recovering from abuse are entitled to be free of male bodies without having to judge each person’s intentions, and that a rule based on self-declared identity cannot keep out the minority of men who would exploit it while putting the burden on women to object. Third spaces and single-occupancy facilities, on this view, can protect transgender people’s privacy too.

The other side holds that transgender women have used women’s facilities for decades in many places, usually unnoticed, and that forcing them into men’s facilities exposes them to harassment and violence and, in practice, shuts them out of work, school and travel. Policing spaces by biology also means policing appearance, so women who look masculine get challenged too, and rare dangerous cases, such as violent offenders, can be handled individually. As of 2026, Britain sets the default at biological sex; many US states and most LGBT organizations set it at gender identity.

questions.text: Do the benefits of puberty blockers and hormones for gender-dysphoric adolescents outweigh the risks?
questions.why: The answer turns on long-term outcomes existing studies were not built to measure: lasting relief from distress, how many would have settled without treatment, and costs to fertility, bones and sexual function.
questions.detail:
Medical bodies have split. US pediatric and endocrine associations support access; health authorities in England, Sweden and Finland restricted it after systematic reviews. Both sides accept that much of the evidence is of moderate or low quality, and read that differently. Supporters say low ratings reflect the near-impossibility of randomized trials in this field, not evidence of harm, that much accepted pediatric care rests on similar evidence, and that observational studies, including long-running Dutch clinic data, report improved mental health and very low regret. Blockers, they argue, pause an irreversible process and buy time, since going through the wrong puberty is itself irreversible.

Skeptics say that when benefits are unproven and harms to fertility, bones and sexual function are known, caution is the ordinary medical standard. Before blockers, most young children with gender dysphoria came to accept their bodies by adulthood, many growing up gay or lesbian; nearly all who start blockers go on to hormones, which suggests blockers set a path rather than buy time. The patient population also shifted after 2010 toward adolescent girls with other mental-health conditions, a group the original Dutch studies did not include. The full clinical debate is on the youth gender transition page.

questions.text: Does letting adults change their legal gender by self-declaration put women at risk in practice?
questions.why: Self-declaration has been law in Argentina since 2012, Denmark since 2014, Ireland since 2015 and Germany since 2024, but the harm at issue is rare events that are hard to count and easy to dispute.
questions.detail:
Opponents argue that a system with no gatekeeping cannot tell a transgender woman from a man who wants access to women, and that it takes only a few such men to cause serious harm in shelters, prisons and changing rooms. Once a person is legally female, staff who exclude them risk discrimination claims, which in practice disarms the people responsible for women’s safety. They point to individual cases, especially in prisons, and hold that the burden of proof lies with those changing a protection women already had.

Supporters answer that the countries with the longest experience show no documented surge of men using legal gender changes to harm women; the number of people changing legal gender is small, and most are transgender people seeking documents that match how they live. Laws against assault, voyeurism and harassment apply regardless of legal gender, and facilities and prisons keep the power to assess individual risk. Medical gatekeeping, as under Britain’s 2004 Act, imposes delay, cost and intrusive scrutiny without stopping anyone determined to abuse the system. How much rides on the answer depends on what legal gender is used for in a given country, which varies widely.

questions.text: Is the rise in young people identifying as transgender mostly acceptance, or mostly social influence?
questions.why: Young people are far likelier than older ones to identify as transgender, and gender clinics saw referrals rise many times over in the 2010s, shifting toward adolescent girls. Data to separate the causes barely exist.
questions.detail:
The two explanations are not exclusive, but they lead to different policies: if the rise mostly reflects people who were always there and now feel safe to say so, recognition is the response; if much of it reflects peer and online influence on distressed adolescents, caution is. Those who stress acceptance note that every stigmatized group, from left-handed people to gay men, grew in visible numbers when stigma lifted, and that older generations grew up when identifying as transgender meant losing family, work and safety. Much of the youth increase is among nonbinary young people who do not seek medical treatment at all. The “social contagion” idea, they argue, rests mostly on surveys of parents recruited from websites skeptical of transition, and echoes old claims that gay identity spreads by influence.

Those who see social influence argue that the scale, speed and concentration of the change among adolescent girls, many with autism, anxiety, depression or trauma, are hard to explain by acceptance alone, and that clinicians in England, Finland and Sweden reported the shift before the politics hardened. Eating disorders and other forms of adolescent distress have shown social patterns, and some young people who transitioned now say online communities influenced them and their underlying problems went untreated.

questions.text: Does legal and social recognition of gender identity improve transgender people’s well-being?
questions.why: Both sides want transgender people’s mental health to improve. Studies link matching documents, chosen names and family acceptance to less distress; critics note most are surveys that cannot show cause.
questions.detail:
Supporters of recognition argue that living without having to disclose a transgender history every time a document is checked removes a constant source of stress and danger, and that the minority-stress model, well established for gay and lesbian people, predicts exactly the associations studies in several countries find. Policies that deny recognition, they say, send a public message of rejection that young people in particular absorb.

Skeptics note that the studies are mostly cross-sectional surveys of self-selected participants, so they cannot tell whether recognition caused better outcomes or reflects families and circumstances that were better to begin with. Much of the distress transgender people report coexists with other conditions that recognition does not treat; registers in Finland and Sweden find poor outcomes persisting after transition, and recognition policies have spread for a decade without a clear improvement across the population. Telling young people that recognition is a matter of life and death, they add, can itself raise the stakes. Causal evidence is scarce on both sides.

questions.text: Should these rules be set by lawmakers and courts, or by sports bodies, schools, doctors and families?
questions.why: As of 2026, much of the change has come from legislatures, executives and courts setting one rule for all. The split does not track left and right neatly: each side wants uniform rules in some arenas and discretion in others.
questions.detail:
Those who favor uniform law argue that when the stakes are fairness for girls, safety in intimate spaces and irreversible treatment of children, the rules should not depend on which school board, sports body or clinic a family happens to deal with. Professional bodies were slow to recognize problems, as England’s Cass Review found of its national gender clinic, and legislatures answer to the public in a way that associations do not. Clear statutory definitions also protect institutions from lawsuits on both sides.

Those who favor discretion argue that one rule cannot fit a middle-school cross-country team and an Olympic final, or a 12-year-old and a 17-year-old with years of distress. Sports bodies know their sports, doctors their patients and parents their children, and politicians writing broad bans, often for electoral advantage, override them all; governing bodies have shown they can draw lines on their own. In the United States, conservatives tend to favor uniform rules on sports and medical care but local discretion on schools, and progressives the reverse.

positions.name: Recognize gender identity in law and shared life
positions.steelman: Transgender people are who they say they are. The law should treat a transgender woman as a woman, on her documents, in the spaces she uses and on the teams she plays for.
positions.detail:
Gender identity is a deep and persistent part of a person, not a preference, and for people whose identity and body conflict, recognition is what makes ordinary life possible. The restrictions spreading across the United States and Britain answer problems that barely exist: transgender people are about 1 percent of Americans 13 and older, the NCAA’s president knew of fewer than 10 transgender athletes in college sports, and countries that have let adults change legal gender by declaration for a decade or more have not seen the harms opponents predicted. What the restrictions do is push transgender people out of work, school, travel, sport and medical care, and tell them they do not belong in public life. The suicide attempts and bullying transgender teenagers report are what stigma and exclusion look like.

Fair competition and privacy are better protected by targeted rules than by blanket exclusion. Sports bodies can set eligibility by sport and level using evidence about individuals; a 2024 IOC-funded laboratory study found transgender women had lower jump height and aerobic capacity relative to body mass than other women. Children’s sport is about taking part, not records. In bathrooms and changing rooms, behavior is what threatens women, and laws against assault, voyeurism and harassment apply to everyone. Women’s rights and transgender rights are not in competition: the rules used to check transgender women end up checking any woman who looks masculine. Most of us favor legal gender by self-declaration and leave medical care for minors to families and clinicians; some accept testosterone limits at elite levels.
positions.proponents: American Civil Liberties Union; Human Rights Campaign; American Academy of Pediatrics; Chase Strangio

positions.name: Use sex where sex matters and protect transgender people
positions.steelman: Sex is real and women’s rights rest on it. Keep sports, changing rooms, shelters and prisons separated by sex, and protect transgender people from discrimination as transgender people.
positions.detail:
Women’s rights were won on the basis of sex, because it is female bodies that get pregnant, that are on average smaller and weaker, and that are the overwhelming majority of victims of male sexual violence. Separate sports, changing rooms, shelters, wards and prisons exist for those reasons, and they work only if “woman” means adult human female. Gender identity is sincere for those who have it, but it cannot be verified, and a law that lets it override sex leaves women unable to say no to any male who identifies into their spaces. Britain’s Supreme Court agreed unanimously in April 2025 that “woman” and “sex” in the Equality Act mean biological woman and biological sex. In January 2026 an employment tribunal found that an NHS trust in Darlington had harassed eight nurses by making them share a changing room with a transgender colleague without a suitable alternative, and in 2023 Scotland changed its prison policy within weeks after a person convicted of two rapes was initially sent to a women’s prison.

None of this denies transgender people dignity. They should be free to live, dress and present as they choose and be protected from discrimination, harassment and violence as transgender people, as UK law already does through gender reassignment. The answer to hard cases is more provision, not redefinition: single-occupancy toilets and changing rooms, third spaces and open sports categories. Many of us are lesbians, feminists and people on the left; some accept gender recognition certificates as a legal fiction for limited purposes, and most favor a cautious, psychology-first approach to minors without backing criminal bans on care.
positions.proponents: Sex Matters; For Women Scotland; J.K. Rowling

positions.name: Make biological sex the only category the law recognizes
positions.steelman: There are two sexes, fixed at conception. The law should say so plainly: record sex, protect sex-based spaces and stop treating a feeling as a legal category.
positions.detail:
“Gender identity” is not a fact about anyone’s body but an ideology that asks everyone else to treat a feeling as more real than biology, and over the 2010s and early 2020s it was written into school curricula, medical practice, federal rules and civil rights law with little public debate. The costs fall on women, who lose fair sports and safe spaces; on children, taught they may be born in the wrong body and steered toward drugs and surgery that cannot be undone; on parents kept in the dark when schools socially transition their children; and on anyone punished for saying the truth about sex. Government should record sex, protect sex-based spaces and opportunities, end public funding for gender transition and protect the freedom to speak, work and raise children by one’s beliefs about sex.

People with gender distress deserve compassion and care, often from counselors and families rather than surgeons, and laws against harassment and assault protect them like everyone else. What we reject is a legal category built on identity that overrides other people’s rights, speech and consciences. Institutions are correcting course: the Supreme Court upheld state limits on medical transition for minors in United States v. Skrmetti in June 2025 and sex-based school sports a year later, and sports governing bodies are moving the same way. Religious conservatives ground this in a view of the person as created male and female; secular conservatives ground it in biology and the protection of women and children.
positions.proponents: Trump administration; Heritage Foundation; Alliance Defending Freedom

positions.name: Recognize gender identity, with sex-based limits in sport
positions.steelman: Transgender people deserve equal dignity, documents, jobs and care. But competitive sport is where the body is the point, so the female category should follow sex.
positions.detail:
Most of the rules being passed against transgender people are cruel and unnecessary. Competitive sport is the exception, because there the body, not identity, is what is being measured: the female category exists to protect women from male physical advantage, which hormones do not fully remove. Saying so is not bigotry, and treating it as bigotry has cost transgender people allies on everything else. Let sports bodies draw lines by sport, age and level, with open participation in children’s recreational play and sex-based categories where competition is serious. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, called transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports “deeply unfair” while condemning “deplorable anti-LGBTQ rhetoric.”

Public opinion fits this settlement better than either pole: 73 percent across 26 countries back protection from discrimination, while 22 percent across 23 back sports by gender identity (Ipsos, 2026), and even among US Democrats, 45 percent favored the birth-sex sports requirement in 2025, up from 37 percent in 2022 (Pew). Performance follows sex; dignity follows how a person lives. Drawing lines domain by domain is how law handles every other hard case, and it is the only approach that can hold a durable majority. Some of us extend sex-based rules to a few other settings, such as prisons for those with violent records; on youth medical care we mostly lean toward parents and doctors deciding.
positions.proponents: Center for American Progress; Gavin Newsom

positions.name: Stop classifying people by sex in law
positions.steelman: The fight over whether the state should record birth sex or gender identity assumes it should record either. It need not, any more than it records religion.
positions.detail:
Race, religion and sexual orientation are not assigned at birth and printed on passports, yet the law still protects people from discrimination on those grounds and collects data where needed. Assigning everyone a legal sex at birth and making it hard to change creates the very conflicts this debate is about, forces transgender and nonbinary people into categories that do not fit, and entrenches the idea that men and women are different kinds of citizen. An “X” marker is not enough, because it marks out the people who choose it. Germany’s national identity card already carries no sex field, and both sides of the fight are struggling over the same document, the birth certificate.

Where a body really matters, in medicine, pregnancy or particular sports, rules can name the physical characteristic or how a person lives rather than a status on a certificate, and data on sex can still be collected where relevant. The Future of Legal Gender project at King’s College London, led by Davina Cooper, spent four years mapping where British law relies on sex or gender and drafted principles for removing legal sex status, while acknowledging that protecting sex-based rights is the main risk of reform. Some of us want sex off birth registration entirely; others only off identity cards and driver’s licenses, and many support self-declared recognition in the meantime.
positions.proponents: Davina Cooper; Future of Legal Gender project; Gender-Free ID Coalition

crux.lead: Where do male and female bodies differ enough that sex, not gender identity, should govern?
crux.subtitle: Most people accept birth sex in some settings and gender identity in others. The fight is over where those lines fall, and who carries the cost of each one: the transgender people a line excludes, or the women and girls a sex-based line protects.
crux.empirical: Some of it can be measured: how much physical advantage remains after male puberty and hormone suppression, by sport, age and level; whether inclusive or sex-based rules for bathrooms, shelters and prisons change rates of assault, harassment and exclusion; how adolescents given puberty blockers and hormones fare over decades against those who are not; and whether recognition improves transgender people’s mental health.
crux.values: No data can say whether legal words like “woman” should name a bodily category or a social identity, or how to weigh the inclusion and dignity of a small group against the fairness, privacy and sense of safety of a larger one when both claims are sincere. One side holds that sex-based protections are the foundation of women’s equality; the other, that being treated as one’s gender is basic to a dignified life.

primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: a large horizontal plastic ID card on a short clip, with a blank empty photo square and blank lines, standing upright on its edge as the dominant focal mass; its corner overlaps a row of three tall changing-room lockers with a slatted bench in front; a stethoscope lies coiled on the bench beside a small sports bag; a single track-and-field hurdle stands on a curving running-track lane that sweeps across the whole frame from lower left to right as the connective element; the ground is a gentle rounded mound with a white margin all round.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #9459a2, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: people, figures, faces, silhouettes, hands, restroom pictograms, gender symbols, transgender symbol, male and female symbols, pride flags, rainbows, pink and blue, protest signs, placards, banners, scales of justice, gavels, question marks, split or half-and-half shapes, mirrors, chromosomes, DNA, pills, syringes, scalpels, crosses, locks, barriers, fences, text, letters.
